title: The 2026 Midterms, in context
text:
THE MIDTERM LEDGER · ELECTION NIGHT TO THE COUNT



Democrats won control of both chambers, ending the Republican trifecta. Some vote counts were still incomplete in the latest reporting used here; estimates and projections are labeled rather than presented as certified totals.

title: The 2026 Midterms, in context
text:
Chamber balance: 2024 to 2026
The 119th Congress convened with narrow Republican control. For the 120th Congress, CBS News projected a Democratic House range of 254–267 seats on Nov. 11 and later projected a 56–44 Democratic Senate after Alaska was called. The House bars show the midpoint of the reported range for visual comparison only; whiskers show its full range.







The 119th Congress composition reflects the post-2024 election starting balance (House: 215 Democrats, 220 Republicans; Senate: 47 Democratic caucus members, 53 Republicans). For 2026, the House range is CBS News’ Nov. 11 estimate and the Senate balance is CBS News’ Nov. 17 projection. Sources: CBS House and Senate overview, CBS Alaska Senate result. The 2026 House non-Democratic range is the mathematical remainder from 435; it is not labeled as an all-Republican count.

title: The 2026 Midterms, in context
section: The president’s party and House losses
text:
The president’s party and House losses
The bars show House seat change for the president’s party at each midterm. The 2026 result is intentionally not plotted as an exact seat swing: available reporting confirms Democratic control but gives a range, not a final certified count.







Historical seat changes are the net change in House seats for the president’s party at midterm elections, compiled from official election results. 2018 is shown as a 41-seat Republican loss, consistent with the final House net change. The 2026 annotation is not a numeric result. Source context: Office of the Historian, U.S. House.

title: The 2026 Midterms, in context
text:
Selected 2026 results
These are projected outcomes reported by CBS News, not a substitute for state-certified canvasses. Percentages are included only where the cited source reported a dated figure; other vote totals are left out rather than inferred.






The 2026 Senate result differs substantially from the earlier scenario numbers sometimes circulated online: CBS reported Democratic wins in Maine, North Carolina, Michigan, Ohio, Georgia, New Hampshire and Texas, while Republicans held Florida. See the CBS results overview and Senate results page. Pennsylvania’s Josh Shapiro is included as a governor’s race; Abigail Spanberger’s Virginia victory was in 2025, not a 2026 midterm race.

title: Turnout and demographic shifts
text: The 2026 midterms had the second-highest turnout rate of any midterm year since 1914, behind 2018, according to political scientist Michael McDonald as cited by the Brennan Center on Nov. 6. A final national rate and a complete set of voter-file records were not available in that report. The demographic comparisons below therefore use only published, clearly defined measures.

title: Turnout and demographic shifts
text:
National turnout trajectory
The chart uses the U.S. Elections Project’s voting-eligible-population (VEP) estimates for 2018 and 2022. The 2026 value is not plotted because a comparable final rate was not available in the cited Nov. 6 reporting; its ranking is stated separately above.







Historical rates: U.S. Elections Project, VEP turnout estimates for 2018 and 2022. 2026 ranking: Brennan Center for Justice, Nov. 6, 2026. The ranking does not supply an exact national percentage.

title: Turnout and demographic shifts
section: Latino voters: presidential vote and House vote
text:
Latino voters: presidential vote and House vote
CBS News exit-poll graphics reported a larger Democratic share among Latino voters in 2026 than in 2024. The comparison is not like-for-like: 2024 is the presidential vote and 2026 is the House vote. Exit polls are estimates, not certified vote counts.







Percentages read from the CBS News national exit-poll graphic for Latino voters. Shares are rounded; omitted percentage points reflect other candidates and rounding.

title: Turnout and demographic shifts
text:
Georgia voter-file participation, by race
Preliminary Georgia voter-file records showed a narrower Black–white turnout gap in 2026 than in any midterm election in the prior 20 years. Brennan Center reported two related cohort measures: the share of 2024 voters who did not return in 2026, and the share of 2026 voters who had also voted in 2024. They have different denominators, shown in separate panels.







Source: Brennan Center for Justice, Nov. 6, 2026. These are Georgia registered-voter-file cohort measures, not national turnout rates or estimates for all eligible residents.

title: Turnout and demographic shifts
text:
Data not yet comparable
This edition does not plot 2026 national turnout by age, education, or urban/suburban/rural residence, nor does it provide a 2018–2026 demographic-margin series. The sources linked here do not provide a complete, consistently defined set of those measures. Exit polls, voter-file participation, and Census turnout rates describe different populations and should not be combined into a single trend without matching definitions.

title: Battlegrounds: what the polls missed
text: This page replaces pre-election scenarios with reported 2026 outcomes. Where public sources do not provide comparable final vote shares or race-level spending figures, those values are omitted rather than estimated.

title: Battlegrounds: what the polls missed
text:
Polling error by state
Pew Research Center compared the final Democratic-minus-Republican polling average with unofficial vote counts as of Nov. 11, 2026. A positive value means the polls understated the Democratic margin. These are signed polling errors, not the candidates’ actual vote margins or poll averages.







Source: Pew Research Center, “A First Look at Polling Performance in 2026”, updated Nov. 12. The results used in its calculations were unofficial counts available Nov. 11; some races were not final.

title: Battlegrounds: what the polls missed
section: How the selected Senate outcomes break down by region
text:
How the selected Senate outcomes break down by region
The eight states below are a selected set, not every competitive Senate contest. The chart counts reported winners by party; it does not represent vote share or regional vote swing.






CBS News projected Democratic wins in Maine (Troy Jackson), North Carolina (Roy Cooper), Michigan (Abdul El-Sayed), Ohio (Sherrod Brown), Georgia (Jon Ossoff), New Hampshire (Chris Pappas), and Texas (James Talarico). Republican Ashley Moody held Florida. See the CBS results overview and Senate results page.

title: Battlegrounds: what the polls missed
text:
Political advertising: cycle-level context
Race-level candidate fundraising, independent expenditures, and vote shares are reported through different systems and periods. The comparable total available here is political advertising, not all campaign or outside spending. AdImpact estimates reported by Deadline put 2026 cycle ad spending at $12.06 billion, versus $11.2 billion in 2024. The two-cycle comparison is context, not evidence that spending caused a result.







Source: Deadline, “Political Ad Spending On 2025–26 Cycle Topped $12 Billion”, citing AdImpact. Ad spending is a media-market estimate and is not interchangeable with FEC candidate receipts, disbursements, or independent expenditures.
